title: What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly.

paper.title: What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly.
paper.abstract:
Abstract A coding agent is a language model wrapped in a harness: the system prompt, the tool set, and the context management that turn a chat model into something that can work inside a repository.
Much of the day-to-day engineering of these agents happens in the harness.
Production harnesses ship releases daily, vendors advertise pass-rate gains from harness changes, and leaderboards mix harnesses freely.
What is rarely measured is how much the harness itself moves the score when the model is held fixed.
This paper measures it.
We run five models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified, and rerun the same configurations to calibrate how much a score moves when nothing changes but the run.
The answer to the title question is: not pass rate.
On 447 tasks and the two models we ran there, Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent, the heaviest and the lightest harness, are equivalent within five points.
On a 45-task hard subset and five models, swapping the harness flips as many tasks as rerunning the same harness, 13% in both cases, and the tasks a harness wins in one run are not the tasks it wins in the next.
The one harness effect that clears the noise is a loss, not a gain: OpenCode trails by up to 9 points on the large pool, and on one model half of that gap sits in runs its output cap cut short.
What the harness does decide is the bill.
With the same model, the same tasks, and one price list, cost per task differs by up to 3 × \times across harnesses.
The gap is set at the first call, by the preamble of system prompt and tool schemas each harness sends with every step, and scaled by the number of steps; per-step growth and per-call tool output differ far less.
The provider’s price for cached input scales the bill and does not reorder it.
The rerun data also give the resolution a harness comparison needs: at the discordance we observe, 45 tasks catch a 13-point gap only half the time and no gap with 80% power, and 447 tasks resolve 5 points, still coarser than the gains many harness changes claim.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Coding agents have turned into a product category, and the product is a model plus a harness. The harness, which part of the literature calls a scaffold, is everything around the model: the system prompt, the tools it can call, the way tool output is fed back, and the way the conversation is trimmed when it grows too long. It is also the part that changes most: popular harnesses ship more than two releases a day ( Ben Sghaier et al., 2026 ) , most of it prompts, tool surfaces, and context management rather than the model. The field has come to believe that this engineering moves the score. The belief has evidence behind it. On a public terminal benchmark, the same model is listed at 52.1% under one harness and 57.8% under another, with the lower-scoring arm consuming 65 × \times the input tokens ( Vats & Golev, 2026 ) . Six harnesses run over the same model pool span 23.8 points ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , and five harnesses on one fixed model span 27.4 points ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Vendors sell harnesses on this basis: one advertises a 2.4-point gain over Claude Code with its own model held fixed ( Zhipu AI, 2026 ) . Leaderboards, meanwhile, mix harnesses freely, so a ranking of models is also a ranking of whatever harness each submitter chose ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . These numbers are hard to read, for two reasons. First, almost all of them come from one run per cell, while ten reruns of one configuration on SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; OpenAI, 2024 ) already spread by 2.2 to 6.0 points ( Bjarnason et al., 2026 ) . Second, the harnesses being compared are often not on the same footing. In the same study, one harness scores 19.1% with a minimal adapter to the benchmark and 73.4% with the full one on the same backbone ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , so part of what such a comparison measures is how well each harness was wired to the benchmark. The study closest to ours shows how much this leaves open. It runs three production harnesses on two models over 50 tasks, one run per cell, and finds within-model differences of 0 to 8 points with intervals that cover zero except the largest, beside a 40 × \times spread in tokens per solved task ( Vats & Golev, 2026 ) . Whether those 8 points come from the harness or from the run cannot be told from that design, since ten reruns of a single configuration already spread by up to 6 points. So the question a harness claim rests on, whether swapping the harness moves a score more than running the same harness again, has not been measured on the same tasks and models. We measure it. We take three production harnesses as they ship, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode ( Anthropic, 2026 ; Lieret et al., 2026 ; Anomaly Innovations, 2026 ) , pin their versions, and run the same models through all three on SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; OpenAI, 2024 ) . The models are Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, and HY4-Preview, with Claude Opus 5 added inside Claude Code as a strong anchor. Of the 492 Verified tasks that run in our offline setup, two sets play different roles. The 45 tasks in the two hardest annotated difficulty bands, all of them, are where we expect a harness to matter most. The remaining 447 give the power to bound a small effect. Ten rerun pairs of the same configuration let the harness gap be read next to the rerun gap, all runs are offline, and every arm is billed under one price list from its own token counts. Held to that standard, the harness barely moves pass rate (Figure 1 ). (a) (b) Figure 1: Same model, different harness. (a) Input tokens per task against pass rate on the 45 hard tasks, one run of every model under every harness. Within a model the harnesses spread two- to three-fold in tokens and stay inside the gap that 45 tasks catch only half the time. (b) Paired pass-rate difference for each pair of harnesses on each model and task set, with 95% intervals for the paired difference; vertical ticks mark the rerun range where a configuration was run more than once. Filled points are the pairs that clear the noise, and all of them are OpenCode trailing on the 447-task pool. On the hard tasks, the spread across the three harnesses is two to five tasks out of 45 for every model, and rerunning one harness moves it by up to three. The two flip the same share of tasks, 13% at the median, and the tasks a harness wins in one run are not the tasks it wins in the next. On the 447 tasks, Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent are equivalent within five points on both models we ran there. We also looked where a harness effect should hide if it existed: a vendor’s own harness on its own model scored inside the range of the other three. What does clear the noise is a loss. OpenCode trails by up to 9 points on the large pool, and half of that gap sits in runs its output cap cut short before a patch was written. Every other harness failure we can name is of the same kind: a hard stop at the context window, a crash at the step cap, a search tool that could not run offline. Every harness effect we can name is a way to lose a task, and none we measured is a way to win one. The harness does decide the bill, and it decides it in a way the pass rate hides. With the same model on the same tasks, cost per task differs by up to 3 × \times across the three harnesses. Little of that comes from what the tools return: per call, the three harnesses hand the model about the same amount of text. It comes from what each harness carries into every step, a fixed preamble of system prompt and tool schemas that is 16k tokens in Claude Code, 7k in OpenCode, and under a thousand in mini-SWE-agent, plus the model’s own reasoning kept in the transcript, which our reconstruction says is re-sent on every turn. The third term is the number of steps the model takes. Step by step, the three contexts then grow at rates within a factor of one and a half of one another, so the bill is set at the first call and multiplied by the step count. The price of cached input scales that bill and does not reorder it: under either vendor’s price list, the three harnesses rank by their tokens. The rerun data also settle what a harness comparison can resolve. At the discordance we observe, 45 tasks catch a 13-point gap half the time and no gap at 80% power, and 447 tasks resolve about 5 points. Many of the published harness gains sit below the first number, and some sit below the second as well.

sections.heading: Harness comparisons.
sections.text: Several recent studies swap whole harnesses under a fixed model and report large spreads. Six configurable harnesses over the same model pool span 23.8 points on a graded task score ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , five harnesses on one model span 27.4 points of Pass@1 ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , and one fixed model costs 139 × \times more tokens under its worst scaffold than under its best on a single git task ( Alier Forment et al., 2026 ) . Two findings in this line point the way we go. Three production harnesses paired on the same terminal tasks differ by 0 to 8 points with intervals that cover zero except the largest, while tokens per solved task differ 40 × \times ( Vats & Golev, 2026 ) , and 35 consecutive releases of one harness bring no significant score gain on a fixed model while nearly doubling token use ( Ben Sghaier et al., 2026 ) . The scaffold papers on SWE-bench before them, SWE-agent, OpenHands, and the agentless pipeline, each compared their own design against the others under a fixed model ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) . Every study in this line runs each cell once or twice. Rankings also move with the harness: which model is most robust to meaning-preserving rewrites of a task depends on whether it runs under mini-SWE-agent or OpenCode ( Mahmud et al., 2026 ) , and a position paper asks that comparisons disclose the harness for this reason ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . We keep the whole-harness unit and the production artifacts, and add the two things this line lacks: reruns of the same cell, and a bill computed under one price list. On pass rate our result agrees with theirs, with the power to bound it.

sections.heading: What is inside a harness.
sections.text: A source-code taxonomy of coding agents lists twelve design dimensions and asks for exactly the control we use, a fixed model with the scaffold varied ( Rombaut, 2026 ) . The three harnesses we run sit at different points of that taxonomy. mini-SWE-agent gives the model a single bash tool and no context management, and reaches SWE-agent’s score in about a hundred lines of Python ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Lieret et al., 2026 ) . Claude Code and OpenCode add typed file tools, long system prompts, and automatic compaction ( Anthropic, 2026 ; Anomaly Innovations, 2026 ) . Component studies show that individual pieces matter under pressure: a context-management package nearly doubles a small model’s score in a 20k-token window ( Lewis, 2026 ) , and restricting the tool surface changes cost by task regime and agent while pass rates stay tied ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . A component study on SWE-bench Verified varies context management, action space, and planning inside one lightweight harness over 176 matched settings, and finds that context management pays as the window tightens and that capable models do as well with a bash-only tool set at lower cost ( Fan et al., 2026 ) . We ask the complementary question: what the whole production harness, as users run it, changes against a rerun of itself. Models fine-tuned on one scaffold’s trajectories lose as much as 29 points when moved to another, while base models vary far less ( Thangarajah et al., 2026 ) . Our check of a vendor’s own harness on its own model is the same question asked of an API model.

sections.heading: Noise and power in agent evaluation.
sections.text: The case for error bars on evaluations has been made for language models in general ( Miller, 2024 ) and for agents in particular, where a score reported without its cost or its variance rewards the wrong things ( Kapoor et al., 2025 ) . Ten reruns of one model–scaffold pair on SWE-bench Verified spread by 2.2 to 6.0 points, with standard deviations above 1.5 points even at temperature zero, so reported gains of 2 to 3 points can be noise ( Bjarnason et al., 2026 ) . A generalizability-theory decomposition finds that the agent main effect explains under 3% of outcome variance while agent-by-task interaction explains 7 to 23% ( Srinivasan, 2026 ) , and a pre-registered comparison on GAIA fits the scaffold-by-model interaction directly and finds it significant ( Starace, 2026 ) . We take the rerun spread as the yardstick, and report every harness gap next to it with the sample size it would take to resolve.

sections.heading: Harnesses.
sections.text: We run three production harnesses as they ship, with the version pinned per arm: Claude Code 2.1 (releases 2.1.259 to 2.1.273 in the scored arms; 2.1.263 on GLM and Opus), mini-SWE-agent 2.4.6, and OpenCode 1.18 (1.18.30 and 1.18.31 in the scored arms; 1.18.30 on GLM) ( Anthropic, 2026 ; Lieret et al., 2026 ; Anomaly Innovations, 2026 ) . The three span the design space of Section 2: one minimal harness and two full products, one closed and one open. They differ in what they give the model. mini-SWE-agent exposes one bash tool, trims only very long observations, and has no context management beyond a hard stop at the model’s window. Claude Code and OpenCode expose typed file, search, and edit tools, prepend long system prompts, and compact the transcript automatically when it grows. None of them sends sampling parameters, so decoding is whatever the provider does by default. We hold one budget fixed across all three: a step is one model call, and every trial gets 300 of them. Wall-clock limits are a safety net, and on the locally served Qwen arms they are not equal: Claude Code, whose steps against vLLM run about twice as slow, could run for 36,000 s where OpenCode’s own soft timeout stopped it at 5,760 s (Appendix A ). On the GLM model, where the API accepts a reasoning-effort setting, all three harnesses pin it to high . Everything else is left as the harness authors set it, and Table A1 in the appendix lists what that is. We also run DeepSeek’s own command-line harness, dsh in the tables, on DeepSeek’s model as a home-field check.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: The ladder has five models that run in all three harnesses: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B, served locally with vLLM 0.27.1 in bfloat16 precision, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (release 0731), GLM-5.3-Flash, and HY4-Preview, called through their vendor APIs (DS Flash, GLM Flash, and HY4 for short in figures and wide tables). The three API models are among the most used on OpenRouter: in its trailing-30-day ranking by tokens processed through 2026-09-20, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 ranks second, HY4-Preview third, and GLM-5.3-Flash fourth ( OpenRouter, 2026 ) . Claude Opus 5 runs inside Claude Code only, through the harness’s own channel, and anchors the top of the ladder. Harbor 0.22.0 ( Harbor Framework Team, 2026 ) orchestrates the runs, one container per trial, and runs the benchmark’s own tests to score each one.

sections.heading: Tasks.
sections.text: SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; OpenAI, 2024 ) has 500 tasks, and 8 of them need a public web service to verify and are dropped, leaving 492. From these we take two disjoint sets. hard45 is every task in the two hardest annotated difficulty bands, 1 to 4 hours and over 4 hours, 42 and 3 tasks, taken whole so that there is no sampling to tune. pool447 is the remaining 447 tasks. Every arm on hard45 runs the same 45 tasks. On pool447 we run the two Qwen models, which we serve ourselves. The agent phase has no network beyond the model endpoint. An audit of our early web-enabled runs found that 71% of DeepSeek and Qwen trials had fetched the upstream fix from GitHub, so those runs are discarded and the condition is enforced at the network layer (Appendix D ). Offline, OpenCode’s search tools fail because they download a binary at first use. We place it ahead of time and report that arm, marked rg in the tables.

sections.heading: Runs and scoring.
sections.text: The quantity we estimate is the difference in pass rate between two harnesses on the same model over the tasks of a set, for one run of each configuration. The reported score of a cell is its first scheduled run of every task, a rule fixed before the results were read. A trial is usable if it was scored and raised no infrastructure exception. Trials that overflowed the window or hit a step, time, or output limit are usable and are scored by the verifier like any other trial, which nearly all of them fail. Where the first run lost a task to infrastructure, the slot is refilled from a rerun of the identical configuration on that task, which never displaces a usable first-run trial (Appendix C ). Tasks with no usable trial are removed from that cell’s denominator, and the count is shown wherever it is below the size of the set. Reruns of the same cell are kept apart and used only to measure how much a score moves on its own. A trial that hits the step cap, the wall-clock limit, the context window, or the output cap is scored as a failure, and we record which of these ended it. Task-level outcomes are paired across harnesses on the same model, so a harness gap is tested with McNemar’s exact test and reported with a Newcombe interval, neither adjusted for the number of pairs. On pool447 we also test equivalence at δ \delta = 5 points with two one-sided tests, which pass when the 90% interval of the difference sits inside ± δ \pm\delta . For each task set we report the smallest gap the exact test detects at 80% power, computed from the discordance we observe, and where no gap reaches that power we say so. Cost is computed from each trial’s own token counts, split into cache-hit input, cache-miss input, and output, under the vendor’s list price for the model. The two vendor-API models in the cost analysis, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash, therefore carry a bill, the locally served models carry token counts only, and Opus runs on a subscription with no per-token price.

sections.heading: 4.2 The noise floor and what it can resolve
sections.text: Figure 2: Swapping the harness flips as many tasks as rerunning the same harness. Each point is one pair of runs on the same tasks, and the value is the share of tasks whose outcome differs between the two. Rerun pairs share model, harness, and settings. Harness pairs share the model. Model pairs share the harness. Filled points are hard45, open points pool447; bars are medians. Swapping the harness flips as many tasks as rerunning the same harness (Figure 2 ). The flip rate of a pair of runs, the share of tasks whose outcome differs between them, puts a rerun, a harness swap, and a model swap on one scale. Reruns on hard45 flip 13% of tasks at the median, and harness swaps flip the same 13%. Swapping the model flips more, 22% at the median, and the pool shows the same picture at a larger n n (Appendix F ). The score moves less than the flip rate because flips go both ways, but the task-level churn from changing the harness is the churn of a rerun. The harness’s flips do not replicate at the task level either. If a harness won a fixed set of tasks, a split in run 1 would repeat in run 2. On the six harness pairs on hard45 run twice on both sides, three on each Qwen model, the split repeats no more often than it reverses: 5 tasks split the same way and 7 the opposite way, the rest tie, and a coin gives that count under either test in Appendix F . A real effect leaves a different trace: for the model swap under the same harness, 10 of 15 such tasks split the same way both times, even though Qwen3.8-27B leads Qwen3.6-35B-A3B by only two to ten tasks on this set. On hard45 the harness gap behaves like a fresh draw of the same noise, with no set of tasks that one harness wins. The flip rates set what a comparison of this kind can resolve. With 14% of tasks discordant between two arms, 45 tasks catch a 12.9-point gap half the time and no gap at 80% power, and 447 tasks detect 5.2 points at that power (Figure A2 in the appendix). So the two-to-five-task gaps in Table 2 cannot be told from zero. By the same scale, a reported gain of a few points needs a paired pool larger than ours, and one read off a single run of a few dozen tasks is inside the noise.

sections.heading: 4.3 A harness can lose tasks
sections.text: Figure 3: How trials end. One bar per model and harness, split into pass, fail with the model stopping on its own, output-token cutoff, context overflow, step or time cap or crash, and trials lost to infrastructure, which are not scored. dsh is DeepSeek’s own harness. The one harness effect that clears the noise is OpenCode losing tasks, and the trajectories say how (Figure 3 ). The first way is an output cap with no recovery: when the model’s reasoning runs past the provider’s cap in the middle of a step, OpenCode does not re-prompt, and a trial cut on its final step ends with whatever is on disk, which is usually nothing. On pool447 with Qwen3.8-27B, 33 OpenCode trials fail this way, where Claude Code, which hits the same cap on the same model and re-prompts the model to continue, loses one. Scoring only the tasks where OpenCode was not cut off roughly halves its gap to the other two harnesses (Table A7 ), and transplanting Claude Code’s recovery prompt into OpenCode recovers tasks at a rate the affected tasks cannot tell from zero (Appendix H ). The rest of OpenCode’s gap goes with a second habit: under OpenCode the model stops sooner. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B over the pool, where no trial is cut off, OpenCode ends after a median of 28 model calls against 71 under mini-SWE-agent and 55 under Claude Code. Its gap to mini-SWE-agent is still +4.7 points. OpenCode also stops soonest on GLM-5.3-Flash (Table A4 ). The data do not say what in OpenCode makes the model stop sooner, only that shorter runs and lost tasks travel together. The other failure modes are also losses, and each traces to one design choice. mini-SWE-agent has no context management, so a long trial runs into the model’s window, which on Qwen3.8-27B happens on 11 of the 45 hard tasks and 18 of the pool. Most of those overflows are symptoms: the other two harnesses mostly failed those tasks too, so a compaction step that recovered the ones another harness passed would move mini-SWE-agent by 6.7 points on the hard tasks and less on the pool, and on rerun most overflow again (Appendix K ). An overflow mostly marks a task the model was already losing. The two full harnesses fail at their own limits instead: Claude Code and OpenCode compact the transcript and lose at most one trial to the window, and Claude Code loses at most two trials per arm at the step cap. OpenCode hits the wall clock on six of the 45 hard tasks on Qwen3.8-27B, where it had a sixth of Claude Code’s time, and dropping those tasks does not shrink its gap there (Table A7 ). OpenCode as shipped also cannot run its search tools offline, and the shipped arm sits lower than the reported arm on one Qwen model and higher on the other (same table). None of these is a way to win a task. The pairs that clear the noise, the filled points in Figure 1 b, all point the same way: toward a harness losing.

sections.heading: 4.4 The harness sets the bill
sections.text: The harness sets the token bill, by up to 3 × \times on the same model (Figure A3 in Appendix G ). A bill is mostly per-step input times steps, and the harness moves both terms. On GLM-5.3-Flash Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent take about as many steps, so their gap is per-step weight: a trial costs 1.81 CNY under Claude Code and 0.97 under mini-SWE-agent, because Claude Code feeds the model most input per step (Table A4 ). OpenCode carries less per step and also stops soonest, so it is cheapest on both counts, at 0.56 CNY. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash the step counts diverge instead: mini-SWE-agent takes 141 steps to Claude Code’s 104, its transcript grows with every one of them, and the lightest harness ends up moving the most tokens. Per-step weight and step count trade against each other, and which one wins depends on the model. The per-step weight is not what the tools return (Table A4 in the appendix). Per call, the three harnesses hand the model about the same amount of text, at the mean and at the 90th percentile. What differs is the preamble each harness carries into every call, its system prompt, tool schemas, and message wrapper: 16,581 tokens in Claude Code, 7,025 in OpenCode, and 829 in mini-SWE-agent, paid again on every step. Claude Code also keeps the model’s own reasoning in the transcript, so a run accumulates many times the model text of a mini-SWE-agent run, and it takes the most steps. Adding these terms to the tool returns and call arguments approximately reconstructs the measured input per step in all three arms (Appendix G gives the gaps). What separates the harnesses’ per-step weight is their own text, not the repository’s. Figure 4: What the model reads at each step. Input tokens of every call against the step index, one faint line per trial and a bold median over the trials still running at that step, drawn while at least half of them are. The harnesses differ first in where the line starts, which is the preamble, and less in how fast it climbs. The cliffs are compactions. Read step by step, the same accounting shows the harnesses separating at the first call (Figure 4 ). The input the model reads rises along a near-straight line in every arm, so a harness is described by where its line starts and how fast it climbs. The harnesses differ first in the start: on GLM-5.3-Flash the first call carries 17.1k tokens under Claude Code, 7.6k under OpenCode, and 1.4k under mini-SWE-agent, and the same three sizes on DeepSeek-V4-Flash. The slopes sit within a factor of one and a half of one another on both models, and the reasoning Claude Code keeps in the transcript accounts for part of its steeper climb (Appendix G ). On DeepSeek-V4-Flash the three lines run nearly parallel, so Claude Code’s per-step input ends up tied with mini-SWE-agent’s and the bill is decided by the step count. Claude Code compacts in a fifth to a third of its trials, at the cliffs in the figure, and mini-SWE-agent never compacts and overflows instead. The first call, the growth per step, and the step count are the three numbers a harness’s bill turns on. The price of a cache hit scales the bill and does not reorder it. Each step re-sends the transcript of the last one, so 96 to 99% of input tokens in every arm on both vendor models are cache hits, and the hit price decides how much of the bill the transcript is. Zhipu charges 0.287 × \times the miss price for a hit, so cached input is most of the GLM bill and Claude Code’s weight shows up as nearly twice mini-SWE-agent’s cost. DeepSeek charges 0.033 × \times , so the cached transcript is under half of the bill and output is as large a term: mini-SWE-agent re-reads more and Claude Code writes more, and the two come out the same. Repricing each model’s tokens under the other vendor’s list keeps the order of the three harnesses in both cases (Appendix G ). What flips Claude Code from cheaper than mini-SWE-agent to twice its cost is the model’s step profile, not the price list.

sections.heading: 4.5 What we looked for and did not find
sections.text: A vendor’s own harness on its own model buys no score advantage. DeepSeek’s harness on DeepSeek-V4-Flash passes 21 of 45, the same as Claude Code and one fewer than mini-SWE-agent, at 1.04 CNY per trial against Claude Code’s 0.98 (Appendix B ). Home field is inside the range on score and at the top of it on bill. Claude Code makes the transcript longer without making the model reason harder. On Qwen3.8-27B over the pool, reasoning is 82.5% of the model’s output under Claude Code and 82.9% under OpenCode, the same share, while total output per trial is 1.23 × \times under Claude Code. Its reasoning grows with the transcript, not faster. The weakest model is not the most harness-sensitive. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B the widest gap that does not involve OpenCode is Claude Code minus mini-SWE-agent, -8.9 points on hard45 ( p p = .39). The next widest is on Qwen3.8-27B, +7.0 points the other way. Both are inside the hard45 noise, the Qwen3.6 gap shrinks on rerun, and on the pool the two harnesses are equivalent within five points on both models. Inside one harness, neither two tool ablations nor a release from a year earlier moves the score. Taking away Claude Code’s file-edit tools, so that Claude Opus 5 edits through bash , and taking away the shell instead both pass within one task of the three control runs (Table A5 ). A release from a year earlier, 1.0.100, also passes within that band, at 0.44 × \times the list-price cost, because it did not enable extended thinking by default. The year-old release moves the bill and not the score. The one interaction we did find is with thinking. Turning it off on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B moves Claude Code and OpenCode by +2.2 and +3.4 points over two runs each, with about as many tasks going up as down, and costs mini-SWE-agent 11 points ( p p = .04; Table A6 ). This suggests that the dependence on thinking belongs to the model and harness pair, not to the model alone.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: What a harness buys, on this evidence, is fewer ways to lose a task, and a bill, not pass rate. Every harness effect we could measure is a way to lose a task the model would otherwise solve: an output cap with no recovery, a context window with no compaction, a search tool that does not run offline. We did not find a harness winning tasks, which puts the engineering where the losses are. The one change that might move a score in our grid is a recovery step for OpenCode’s output cutoff, which Claude Code already has. Transplanted, it recovered tasks at a rate that 41 tasks cannot tell from zero, because the runaway reasoning behind the cut recurs on only about 15% of reruns of the same task. The three harnesses differ most in the parts that get the most attention, the prompt, the tool surface, the compaction policy, and none of those differences buys a score gain. The thinking interaction is the one lead we would chase. Switching thinking off on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B costs mini-SWE-agent 11 points and moves the other two by less than the noise. On HY4-Preview, however, the same switch inside Claude Code costs 11 points, as much as the widest harness gap on that model, and cuts output tokens by more than half. The two results suggest that dependence on explicit reasoning is specific to the model and harness pair, but our grid is too small to identify the mechanism. Two limits on scope. Our results come from one benchmark. The one-model check on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Appendix L ) is a transfer check, and general-purpose agents may be a different regime. And the closed anchor model runs in Claude Code only, so the three-harness ladder stops at HY4-Preview and cannot tell whether a closed frontier model shows the same gaps. Swapping the harness under a fixed model moves pass rate on SWE-bench Verified by as much as rerunning the same harness on the 45 hardest tasks, across five models. On the 447-task pool, the pairs that clear the noise are all OpenCode trailing, by 8 to 9 points on Qwen3.8-27B, tied to how it ends a trial. What the harness does decide is the bill, by up to 3 × \times on the same model, through what it carries into each step and how many steps the model takes, and the cache price scales that bill without reordering it. The numbers to carry between vendors are the first call, the growth per step, and the step count. At the discordance we observe, a harness comparison on 45 tasks catches a 12.9-point gap half the time and nothing at 80% power, and on 447 tasks it resolves 5.2 points. The cheapest control in such a comparison is a second run of the same cell, the one most comparisons skip, and we recommend reporting it next to any harness gap.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: All tasks come from the public SWE-bench Verified benchmark, and no human subjects or personal data are involved. The upstream fixes that networked agents retrieved are public GitHub content; we report retrieval rates by model to inform evaluation practice and make no claim that any vendor trained on or intended to use the test data. API keys and credentials were removed from all released files.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: Every number in the paper is generated from one table of trials by the scripts that draw the figures and tables, and Appendix A lists the harness versions, the settings each arm ran with, and how the offline condition was enforced. sections.heading: Budget.
sections.text: Every trial has a cap of 300 steps, set through each harness’s own knob: --max-turns in Claude Code, step_limit in mini-SWE-agent, build.steps in OpenCode. Wall-clock limits are kept only as a safety net. On the locally served Qwen arms Harbor’s multiplier on the task’s 3,000 s agent timeout is six for mini-SWE-agent and OpenCode and twelve for Claude Code, whose prefix-cache pattern against vLLM makes each step about twice as slow; OpenCode’s run command also carries its own soft timeout of 5,760 s, and that is the limit that binds. On the vendor-API arms one soft timeout applies to every harness, 2,760 s on DeepSeek and Opus and 5,760 s on GLM. The asymmetry costs OpenCode six trials on Qwen3.8-27B × \times hard45: nine of its trials hit the soft timeout at 5,760 s, where Claude Code could run to 36,000 s, and six of them failed. All six were still making tool calls with a patch on disk, none was near the step cap, and we report this as an uncontrolled factor rather than a harness effect. A trial that reaches either limit is scored as a failure.

sections.heading: Context window.
sections.text: The two Qwen models are served with a 131k-token window. OpenCode is configured with an input limit of 98k tokens and an output limit of 32k, so the two together fit the window; it compacts when the conversation exceeds the input limit minus a 20k reserve, at about 78k tokens. On the Qwen arms Claude Code’s auto-compaction window is set to 110k, which fires at a measured median of 78k tokens, matching OpenCode by construction; on the vendor-API arms Claude Code runs with its default window and compacts much later, on GLM-5.3-Flash at a median of 168k prompt tokens. mini-SWE-agent has no compaction and runs into the model’s window; that outcome is reported as its own column.

sections.heading: Network.
sections.text: The agent phase of every reported run has no network beyond the model endpoint and the host’s package mirror. On the servers this is Harbor’s allowlist mode, which puts the trial container behind an egress sidecar. The Opus runs, which must run on a local machine with the subscription channel, use an internal Docker network and a phase-aware proxy that admits only the model API during the agent phase and any host during verification; every denial is logged, and a content-level audit found no scored trial in any offline arm that retrieved GitHub content. Two harness-specific consequences of the offline condition are handled explicitly. OpenCode downloads ripgrep at first use, so its grep and glob tools fail offline; the reported arm pre-places the binary, and the shipped arm is kept for Table A7 . mini-SWE-agent calls the model without streaming, and the egress sidecar drops plain-HTTP connections that do not answer within 15 seconds, so its local-model arms go through a TLS forwarder on the host; this changes transport, not sampling.

sections.heading: Other fixed conditions.
sections.text: OpenCode selects its system prompt by model-name pattern, and every model in this study falls into its default prompt. Claude Code runs with a fresh configuration directory per trial and with web search disallowed; against non-Anthropic endpoints its Grep tool is unavailable, and those arms search through Bash . Thinking is on by default in every reported arm, including the three HY4-Preview arms, which are called through the vendor’s API. The Qwen3.6-35B-A3B thinking-off arms of Appendix J switch it off at the serving layer, so the switch is the same for all three harnesses; the HY4-Preview thinking-off arm switches it off through the API’s thinking field, which the endpoint treats as on when it is missing, and it runs in Claude Code only. For the HY4-Preview Claude Code arms the reverse proxy folds Claude Code’s mid-conversation system messages into the preceding user message and sets the thinking field explicitly, which aligns the vendor endpoint with the defaults of the Anthropic API; the content and the order of the conversation are unchanged. Claude Code sends a reasoning-effort setting of xhigh to every endpoint; vLLM’s Anthropic-compatible endpoint ignores it, and on the Qwen arms the reasoning per step under Claude Code is within a few percent of OpenCode’s, which sends none.

sections.heading: Appendix B DeepSeek’s own harness
sections.text: The home-field arm runs DeepSeek’s command-line harness, release 0.1.2-rc.1, on DeepSeek-V4-Flash over hard45, driven by Harbor like the other three and under the same soft timeout. All 45 trials were scored, none was lost to infrastructure, and 21 passed, the same count as Claude Code on the same model. Six trials ended with a non-zero exit from the harness, three of them after a passing patch. The harness takes 111.2 model calls per trial, between OpenCode’s 88.2 and mini-SWE-agent’s 141.1 on this model, and costs 1.04 CNY per trial at DeepSeek’s list price, two fen above mini-SWE-agent, the most expensive of the three general harnesses on this model. A vendor’s own harness lands inside the range of the three general ones on score and at the top of it on bill.

sections.heading: Appendix D Leakage audit of the web-enabled runs
sections.text: Before the offline condition was enforced, the DeepSeek and Qwen arms ran with network access. An audit of those runs scanned tool-call arguments for retrieval of the upstream fix: a GitHub search hit, a commit patch, a pull-request diff, or the post-fix file from the raw content host. 312 of 439 trials had fetched the fix, 152 of them citing the task’s own issue or pull-request number, and 310 of the 312 went on to edit a file after the lookup. The Claude models did this in 4 of 445 trials. Pass rate followed: 96% of the scored DeepSeek and Qwen trials that retrieved the fix passed, against 71% of those that never touched the network. All web-enabled pass-rate results were discarded, and the condition was moved from the prompt to the network layer.

sections.heading: Appendix F Resolution of a paired comparison
sections.text: The flip rate of a pair of runs is the share of tasks whose outcome differs between them, ( b + c ) / n (b+c)/n in the notation of Table 1 . Across the ten rerun pairs on hard45 the median flip rate is 13%, and 16% over the 7 pairs on the five ladder models, since Claude Opus 5’s three reruns are the quietest; across the 15 harness pairs it is 13%, and across the model pairs 22% at the median and up to 56%. On pool447 the one rerun pair flips 13% of tasks and the six harness pairs flip 9 to 16%. The replication test of Section 4.2 starts from the 41 run-1 splits of the six twice-run harness pairs, on 16 distinct tasks; among the 12 tasks split in both runs, 5 same and 7 opposite give a binomial p p = .77, and p p = .821 under a permutation that flips the sign of a whole task at once. The smallest paired difference the exact McNemar test detects at 80% power depends on n n and on the discordance rate; Figure A2 plots it at the 14% we observe pooled over the harness pairs, with a band for the range across pairs. Power is unconditional: the number of discordant tasks is binomial in n n and the discordance rate, and given that number the two-sided exact test at α \alpha = .05 rejects or not. Fewer than six discordant tasks split one way cannot reject at all, so below 55 tasks no difference reaches 80% power at this discordance; at 45 tasks the ceiling is 62%, reached when every discordant task points the same way. The asymptotic formula that inverts the usual sample-size expression is drawn dashed for reference and is optimistic by half a point to a point everywhere. The equivalence verdicts on pool447 rest on the 90% interval of the Claude Code minus mini-SWE-agent difference, [-4.7, +1.1] on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and [-3.7, +1.0] on Qwen3.8-27B, both inside ± \pm 5. Figure A2: Smallest detectable paired difference against sample size. Exact McNemar test at α \alpha = .05 and 80% power, at the pooled discordance rate (solid line) and across the range observed between harness pairs (band); the asymptotic formula is dashed. At 45 tasks no difference reaches 80% power.

sections.heading: Appendix H The output cutoff and a recovery transplant
sections.text: OpenCode’s provider configuration caps a single response at 32k output tokens, and the trajectories show the cut landing at exactly that size in the middle of a reasoning block. On pool447 with Qwen3.8-27B, 38 of 447 OpenCode trials contain such a cut and in 34 of them it is the final step, all but one of which fail. Those trials pass at 7.9% against 75.9% for the rest, and 32 of the 34 end with the repository untouched, after a median of 11 steps. Claude Code on the same model and pool is cut in 52 of 447 trials, 66 events in all; 64 of them are followed by the harness’s own resume prompt and the session continues, and one trial ends on the cap. Its trials with a cut pass at 69% against 79% without. mini-SWE-agent never reaches the cap; its largest single step is 13k output tokens. To test whether the recovery prompt is the difference, we patched Harbor’s OpenCode wrapper to re-invoke the session with Claude Code’s resume string, verbatim, whenever the last step was cut or the repository was untouched, and reran the 41 pool447 tasks whose parent trial had failed that way under both the stock and the patched wrapper, two attempts each, interleaved on one host. Mean per-task reward is 0.585 stock and 0.634 with recovery; six tasks improve, two worsen, 33 tie ( p p = .29, exact sign test). The prompt fired on 15% of the patched trials, against the 33 of 41 parent trials that had been cut, so the failure belongs to the run rather than to the task. Recovery cost 1.23 × \times the steps and 1.30 × \times the input tokens.

Affiliation: Shandong University Email: zhongyi.han@sdu.edu.cn Abstract A coding agent is a language model wrapped in a harness: the system prompt, the tool set, and the context management that turn a chat model into something that can work inside a repository. Much of the day-to-day engineering of these agents happens in the harness. Production harnesses ship releases daily, vendors advertise pass-rate gains from harness changes, and leaderboards mix harnesses freely. What is rarely measured is how much the harness itself moves the score when the model is held fixed. This paper measures it. We run five models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified, and rerun the same configurations to calibrate how much a score moves when nothing changes but the run. The answer to the title question is: not pass rate. On 447 tasks and the two models we ran there, Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent, the heaviest and the lightest harness, are equivalent within five points. On a 45-task hard subset and five models, swapping the harness flips as many tasks as rerunning the same harness, 13% in both cases, and the tasks a harness wins in one run are not the tasks it wins in the next. The one harness effect that clears the noise is a loss, not a gain: OpenCode trails by up to 9 points on the large pool, and on one model half of that gap sits in runs its output cap cut short. What the harness does decide is the bill. With the same model, the same tasks, and one price list, cost per task differs by up to 3 × \times across harnesses. The gap is set at the first call, by the preamble of system prompt and tool schemas each harness sends with every step, and scaled by the number of steps; per-step growth and per-call tool output differ far less. The provider’s price for cached input scales the bill and does not reorder it. The rerun data also give the resolution a harness comparison needs: at the discordance we observe, 45 tasks catch a 13-point gap only half the time and no gap with 80% power, and 447 tasks resolve 5 points, still coarser than the gains many harness changes claim. 1 Introduction Coding agents have turned into a product category, and the product is a model plus a harness. The harness, which part of the literature calls a scaffold, is everything around the model: the system prompt, the tools it can call, the way tool output is fed back, and the way the conversation is trimmed when it grows too long. It is also the part that changes most: popular harnesses ship more than two releases a day ( Ben Sghaier et al., 2026 ) , most of it prompts, tool surfaces, and context management rather than the model. The field has come to believe that this engineering moves the score. The belief has evidence behind it. On a public terminal benchmark, the same model is listed at 52.1% under one harness and 57.8% under another, with the lower-scoring arm consuming 65 × \times the input tokens ( Vats & Golev, 2026 ) . Six harnesses run over the same model pool span 23.8 points ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , and five harnesses on one fixed model span 27.4 points ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Vendors sell harnesses on this basis: one advertises a 2.4-point gain over Claude Code with its own model held fixed ( Zhipu AI, 2026 ) . Leaderboards, meanwhile, mix harnesses freely, so a ranking of models is also a ranking of whatever harness each submitter chose ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . These numbers are hard to read, for two reasons. First, almost all of them come from one run per cell, while ten reruns of one configuration on SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; OpenAI, 2024 ) already spread by 2.2 to 6.0 points ( Bjarnason et al., 2026 ) . Second, the harnesses being compared are often not on the same footing. In the same study, one harness scores 19.1% with a minimal adapter to the benchmark and 73.4% with the full one on the same backbone ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , so part of what such a comparison measures is how well each harness was wired to the benchmark. The study closest to ours shows how much this leaves open. It runs three production harnesses on two models over 50 tasks, one run per cell, and finds within-model differences of 0 to 8 points with intervals that cover zero except the largest, beside a 40 × \times spread in tokens per solved task ( Vats & Golev, 2026 ) . Whether those 8 points come from the harness or from the run cannot be told from that design, since ten reruns of a single configuration already spread by up to 6 points. So the question a harness claim rests on, whether swapping the harness moves a score more than running the same harness again, has not been measured on the same tasks and models. We measure it. We take three production harnesses as they ship, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode ( Anthropic, 2026 ; Lieret et al., 2026 ; Anomaly Innovations, 2026 ) , pin their versions, and run the same models through all three on SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; OpenAI, 2024 ) . The models are Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, and HY4-Preview, with Claude Opus 5 added inside Claude Code as a strong anchor. Of the 492 Verified tasks that run in our offline setup, two sets play different roles. The 45 tasks in the two hardest annotated difficulty bands, all of them, are where we expect a harness to matter most. The remaining 447 give the power to bound a small effect. Ten rerun pairs of the same configuration let the harness gap be read next to the rerun gap, all runs are offline, and every arm is billed under one price list from its own token counts. Held to that standard, the harness barely moves pass rate (Figure 1 ). (a) (b) Figure 1: Same model, different harness. (a) Input tokens per task against pass rate on the 45 hard tasks, one run of every model under every harness. Little of that comes from what the tools return: per call, the three harnesses hand the model about the same amount of text. It comes from what each harness carries into every step, a fixed preamble of system prompt and tool schemas that is 16k tokens in Claude Code, 7k in OpenCode, and under a thousand in mini-SWE-agent, plus the model’s own reasoning kept in the transcript, which our reconstruction says is re-sent on every turn. The third term is the number of steps the model takes. Step by step, the three contexts then grow at rates within a factor of one and a half of one another, so the bill is set at the first call and multiplied by the step count. The price of cached input scales that bill and does not reorder it: under either vendor’s price list, the three harnesses rank by their tokens. The rerun data also settle what a harness comparison can resolve. At the discordance we observe, 45 tasks catch a 13-point gap half the time and no gap at 80% power, and 447 tasks resolve about 5 points. Many of the published harness gains sit below the first number, and some sit below the second as well. 2 Related Work Harness comparisons. Several recent studies swap whole harnesses under a fixed model and report large spreads. Six configurable harnesses over the same model pool span 23.8 points on a graded task score ( Yao et al., 2026 ) , five harnesses on one model span 27.4 points of Pass@1 ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , and one fixed model costs 139 × \times more tokens under its worst scaffold than under its best on a single git task ( Alier Forment et al., 2026 ) . Two findings in this line point the way we go. Three production harnesses paired on the same terminal tasks differ by 0 to 8 points with intervals that cover zero except the largest, while tokens per solved task differ 40 × \times ( Vats & Golev, 2026 ) , and 35 consecutive releases of one harness bring no significant score gain on a fixed model while nearly doubling token use ( Ben Sghaier et al., 2026 ) . The scaffold papers on SWE-bench before them, SWE-agent, OpenHands, and the agentless pipeline, each compared their own design against the others under a fixed model ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) . Every study in this line runs each cell once or twice. Rankings also move with the harness: which model is most robust to meaning-preserving rewrites of a task depends on whether it runs under mini-SWE-agent or OpenCode ( Mahmud et al., 2026 ) , and a position paper asks that comparisons disclose the harness for this reason ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . We keep the whole-harness unit and the production artifacts, and add the two things this line lacks: reruns of the same cell, and a bill computed under one price list. On pass rate our result agrees with theirs, with the power to bound it. What is inside a harness. A source-code taxonomy of coding agents lists twelve design dimensions and asks for exactly the control we use, a fixed model with the scaffold varied ( Rombaut, 2026 ) . The three harnesses we run sit at different points of that taxonomy. mini-SWE-agent gives the model a single bash tool and no context management, and reaches SWE-agent’s score in about a hundred lines of Python ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Lieret et al., 2026 ) . Claude Code and OpenCode add typed file tools, long system prompts, and automatic compaction ( Anthropic, 2026 ; Anomaly Innovations, 2026 ) . Component studies show that individual pieces matter under pressure: a context-management package nearly doubles a small model’s score in a 20k-token window ( Lewis, 2026 ) , and restricting the tool surface changes cost by task regime and agent while pass rates stay tied ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . A component study on SWE-bench Verified varies context management, action space, and planning inside one lightweight harness over 176 matched settings, and finds that context management pays as the window tightens and that capable models do as well with a bash-only tool set at lower cost ( Fan et al., 2026 ) . We ask the complementary question: what the whole production harness, as users run it, changes against a rerun of itself. Models fine-tuned on one scaffold’s trajectories lose as much as 29 points when moved to another, while base models vary far less ( Thangarajah et al., 2026 ) . Our check of a vendor’s own harness on its own model is the same question asked of an API model. Noise and power in agent evaluation. The case for error bars on evaluations has been made for language models in general ( Miller, 2024 ) and for agents in particular, where a score reported without its cost or its variance rewards the wrong things ( Kapoor et al., 2025 ) . Ten reruns of one model–scaffold pair on SWE-bench Verified spread by 2.2 to 6.0 points, with standard deviations above 1.5 points even at temperature zero, so reported gains of 2 to 3 points can be noise ( Bjarnason et al., 2026 ) . A generalizability-theory decomposition finds that the agent main effect explains under 3% of outcome variance while agent-by-task interaction explains 7 to 23% ( Srinivasan, 2026 ) , and a pre-registered comparison on GAIA fits the scaffold-by-model interaction directly and finds it significant ( Starace, 2026 ) . We take the rerun spread as the yardstick, and report every harness gap next to it with the sample size it would take to resolve. 3 Setup Harnesses. We run three production harnesses as they ship, with the version pinned per arm: Claude Code 2.1 (releases 2.1.259 to 2.1.273 in the scored arms; 2.1.263 on GLM and Opus), mini-SWE-agent 2.4.6, and OpenCode 1.18 (1.18.30 and 1.18.31 in the scored arms; 1.18.30 on GLM) ( Anthropic, 2026 ; Lieret et al., 2026 ; Anomaly Innovations, 2026 ) . The three span the design space of Section 2: one minimal harness and two full products, one closed and one open. They differ in what they give the model. mini-SWE-agent exposes one bash tool, trims only very long observations, and has no context management beyond a hard stop at the model’s window. Claude Code and OpenCode expose typed file, search, and edit tools, prepend long system prompts, and compact the transcript automatically when it grows. None of them sends sampling parameters, so decoding is whatever the provider does by default. We hold one budget fixed across all three: a step is one model call, and every trial gets 300 of them. Wall-clock limits are a safety net, and on the locally served Qwen arms they are not equal: Claude Code, whose steps against vLLM run about twice as slow, could run for 36,000 s where OpenCode’s own soft timeout stopped it at 5,760 s (Appendix A ). On the GLM model, where the API accepts a reasoning-effort setting, all three harnesses pin it to high . Everything else is left as the harness authors set it, and Table A1 in the appendix lists what that is. We also run DeepSeek’s own command-line harness, dsh in the tables, on DeepSeek’s model as a home-field check. Models. The ladder has five models that run in all three harnesses: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B, served locally with vLLM 0.27.1 in bfloat16 precision, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (release 0731), GLM-5.3-Flash, and HY4-Preview, called through their vendor APIs (DS Flash, GLM Flash, and HY4 for short in figures and wide tables). The three API models are among the most used on OpenRouter: in its trailing-30-day ranking by tokens processed through 2026-09-20, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 ranks second, HY4-Preview third, and GLM-5.3-Flash fourth ( OpenRouter, 2026 ) . Claude Opus 5 runs inside Claude Code only, through the harness’s own channel, and anchors the top of the ladder. Harbor 0.22.0 ( Harbor Framework Team, 2026 ) orchestrates the runs, one container per trial, and runs the benchmark’s own tests to score each one. Tasks. SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; OpenAI, 2024 ) has 500 tasks, and 8 of them need a public web service to verify and are dropped, leaving 492. From these we take two disjoint sets. hard45 is every task in the two hardest annotated difficulty bands, 1 to 4 hours and over 4 hours, 42 and 3 tasks, taken whole so that there is no sampling to tune. pool447 is the remaining 447 tasks. Every arm on hard45 runs the same 45 tasks. On pool447 we run the two Qwen models, which we serve ourselves. The agent phase has no network beyond the model endpoint. An audit of our early web-enabled runs found that 71% of DeepSeek and Qwen trials had fetched the upstream fix from GitHub, so those runs are discarded and the condition is enforced at the network layer (Appendix D ). Offline, OpenCode’s search tools fail because they download a binary at first use. We place it ahead of time and report that arm, marked rg in the tables. Runs and scoring. The quantity we estimate is the difference in pass rate between two harnesses on the same model over the tasks of a set, for one run of each configuration. The reported score of a cell is its first scheduled run of every task, a rule fixed before the results were read. A trial is usable if it was scored and raised no infrastructure exception. Trials that overflowed the window or hit a step, time, or output limit are usable and are scored by the verifier like any other trial, which nearly all of them fail. Where the first run lost a task to infrastructure, the slot is refilled from a rerun of the identical configuration on that task, which never displaces a usable first-run trial (Appendix C ). Tasks with no usable trial are removed from that cell’s denominator, and the count is shown wherever it is below the size of the set. Reruns of the same cell are kept apart and used only to measure how much a score moves on its own. A trial that hits the step cap, the wall-clock limit, the context window, or the output cap is scored as a failure, and we record which of these ended it. Task-level outcomes are paired across harnesses on the same model, so a harness gap is tested with McNemar’s exact test and reported with a Newcombe interval, neither adjusted for the number of pairs. On pool447 we also test equivalence at δ \delta = 5 points with two one-sided tests, which pass when the 90% interval of the difference sits inside ± δ \pm\delta . For each task set we report the smallest gap the exact test detects at 80% power, computed from the discordance we observe, and where no gap reaches that power we say so. Cost is computed from each trial’s own token counts, split into cache-hit input, cache-miss input, and output, under the vendor’s list price for the model. The two vendor-API models in the cost analysis, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash, therefore carry a bill, the locally served models carry token counts only, and Opus runs on a subscription with no per-token price. 4 Results 4.1 The harness barely moves pass rate Table 1: Paired comparison on pool447. Swapping the harness flips as many tasks as rerunning the same harness (Figure 2 ). The flip rate of a pair of runs, the share of tasks whose outcome differs between them, puts a rerun, a harness swap, and a model swap on one scale. Reruns on hard45 flip 13% of tasks at the median, and harness swaps flip the same 13%. Swapping the model flips more, 22% at the median, and the pool shows the same picture at a larger n n (Appendix F ). The score moves less than the flip rate because flips go both ways, but the task-level churn from changing the harness is the churn of a rerun. The harness’s flips do not replicate at the task level either. If a harness won a fixed set of tasks, a split in run 1 would repeat in run 2. On the six harness pairs on hard45 run twice on both sides, three on each Qwen model, the split repeats no more often than it reverses: 5 tasks split the same way and 7 the opposite way, the rest tie, and a coin gives that count under either test in Appendix F . A real effect leaves a different trace: for the model swap under the same harness, 10 of 15 such tasks split the same way both times, even though Qwen3.8-27B leads Qwen3.6-35B-A3B by only two to ten tasks on this set. By the same scale, a reported gain of a few points needs a paired pool larger than ours, and one read off a single run of a few dozen tasks is inside the noise. 4.3 A harness can lose tasks Figure 3: How trials end. The one harness effect that clears the noise is OpenCode losing tasks, and the trajectories say how (Figure 3 ). The first way is an output cap with no recovery: when the model’s reasoning runs past the provider’s cap in the middle of a step, OpenCode does not re-prompt, and a trial cut on its final step ends with whatever is on disk, which is usually nothing. On pool447 with Qwen3.8-27B, 33 OpenCode trials fail this way, where Claude Code, which hits the same cap on the same model and re-prompts the model to continue, loses one. Scoring only the tasks where OpenCode was not cut off roughly halves its gap to the other two harnesses (Table A7 ), and transplanting Claude Code’s recovery prompt into OpenCode recovers tasks at a rate the affected tasks cannot tell from zero (Appendix H ). The rest of OpenCode’s gap goes with a second habit: under OpenCode the model stops sooner. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B over the pool, where no trial is cut off, OpenCode ends after a median of 28 model calls against 71 under mini-SWE-agent and 55 under Claude Code. Its gap to mini-SWE-agent is still +4.7 points. OpenCode also stops soonest on GLM-5.3-Flash (Table A4 ). The data do not say what in OpenCode makes the model stop sooner, only that shorter runs and lost tasks travel together. The other failure modes are also losses, and each traces to one design choice. mini-SWE-agent has no context management, so a long trial runs into the model’s window, which on Qwen3.8-27B happens on 11 of the 45 hard tasks and 18 of the pool. Most of those overflows are symptoms: the other two harnesses mostly failed those tasks too, so a compaction step that recovered the ones another harness passed would move mini-SWE-agent by 6.7 points on the hard tasks and less on the pool, and on rerun most overflow again (Appendix K ). An overflow mostly marks a task the model was already losing. The two full harnesses fail at their own limits instead: Claude Code and OpenCode compact the transcript and lose at most one trial to the window, and Claude Code loses at most two trials per arm at the step cap. OpenCode hits the wall clock on six of the 45 hard tasks on Qwen3.8-27B, where it had a sixth of Claude Code’s time, and dropping those tasks does not shrink its gap there (Table A7 ). A bill is mostly per-step input times steps, and the harness moves both terms. On GLM-5.3-Flash Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent take about as many steps, so their gap is per-step weight: a trial costs 1.81 CNY under Claude Code and 0.97 under mini-SWE-agent, because Claude Code feeds the model most input per step (Table A4 ). OpenCode carries less per step and also stops soonest, so it is cheapest on both counts, at 0.56 CNY. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash the step counts diverge instead: mini-SWE-agent takes 141 steps to Claude Code’s 104, its transcript grows with every one of them, and the lightest harness ends up moving the most tokens. Per-step weight and step count trade against each other, and which one wins depends on the model. The per-step weight is not what the tools return (Table A4 in the appendix). Per call, the three harnesses hand the model about the same amount of text, at the mean and at the 90th percentile. What differs is the preamble each harness carries into every call, its system prompt, tool schemas, and message wrapper: 16,581 tokens in Claude Code, 7,025 in OpenCode, and 829 in mini-SWE-agent, paid again on every step. Claude Code also keeps the model’s own reasoning in the transcript, so a run accumulates many times the model text of a mini-SWE-agent run, and it takes the most steps. Adding these terms to the tool returns and call arguments approximately reconstructs the measured input per step in all three arms (Appendix G gives the gaps). DeepSeek’s harness on DeepSeek-V4-Flash passes 21 of 45, the same as Claude Code and one fewer than mini-SWE-agent, at 1.04 CNY per trial against Claude Code’s 0.98 (Appendix B ). Home field is inside the range on score and at the top of it on bill. Claude Code makes the transcript longer without making the model reason harder. On Qwen3.8-27B over the pool, reasoning is 82.5% of the model’s output under Claude Code and 82.9% under OpenCode, the same share, while total output per trial is 1.23 × \times under Claude Code. Its reasoning grows with the transcript, not faster. The weakest model is not the most harness-sensitive. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B the widest gap that does not involve OpenCode is Claude Code minus mini-SWE-agent, -8.9 points on hard45 ( p p = .39). The next widest is on Qwen3.8-27B, +7.0 points the other way. Both are inside the hard45 noise, the Qwen3.6 gap shrinks on rerun, and on the pool the two harnesses are equivalent within five points on both models. Inside one harness, neither two tool ablations nor a release from a year earlier moves the score. Taking away Claude Code’s file-edit tools, so that Claude Opus 5 edits through bash , and taking away the shell instead both pass within one task of the three control runs (Table A5 ). A release from a year earlier, 1.0.100, also passes within that band, at 0.44 × \times the list-price cost, because it did not enable extended thinking by default. The year-old release moves the bill and not the score. The one interaction we did find is with thinking. Turning it off on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B moves Claude Code and OpenCode by +2.2 and +3.4 points over two runs each, with about as many tasks going up as down, and costs mini-SWE-agent 11 points ( p p = .04; Table A6 ). This suggests that the dependence on thinking belongs to the model and harness pair, not to the model alone. 5 Discussion and Conclusion What a harness buys, on this evidence, is fewer ways to lose a task, and a bill, not pass rate. Every harness effect we could measure is a way to lose a task the model would otherwise solve: an output cap with no recovery, a context window with no compaction, a search tool that does not run offline. We did not find a harness winning tasks, which puts the engineering where the losses are. The one change that might move a score in our grid is a recovery step for OpenCode’s output cutoff, which Claude Code already has. Transplanted, it recovered tasks at a rate that 41 tasks cannot tell from zero, because the runaway reasoning behind the cut recurs on only about 15% of reruns of the same task. The three harnesses differ most in the parts that get the most attention, the prompt, the tool surface, the compaction policy, and none of those differences buys a score gain. The thinking interaction is the one lead we would chase. Switching thinking off on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B costs mini-SWE-agent 11 points and moves the other two by less than the noise. On HY4-Preview, however, the same switch inside Claude Code costs 11 points, as much as the widest harness gap on that model, and cuts output tokens by more than half. The two results suggest that dependence on explicit reasoning is specific to the model and harness pair, but our grid is too small to identify the mechanism. Two limits on scope. Our results come from one benchmark. The one-model check on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Appendix L ) is a transfer check, and general-purpose agents may be a different regime. And the closed anchor model runs in Claude Code only, so the three-harness ladder stops at HY4-Preview and cannot tell whether a closed frontier model shows the same gaps. Swapping the harness under a fixed model moves pass rate on SWE-bench Verified by as much as rerunning the same harness on the 45 hardest tasks, across five models. On the 447-task pool, the pairs that clear the noise are all OpenCode trailing, by 8 to 9 points on Qwen3.8-27B, tied to how it ends a trial. What the harness does decide is the bill, by up to 3 × \times on the same model, through what it carries into each step and how many steps the model takes, and the cache price scales that bill without reordering it. The numbers to carry between vendors are the first call, the growth per step, and the step count. At the discordance we observe, a harness comparison on 45 tasks catches a 12.9-point gap half the time and nothing at 80% power, and on 447 tasks it resolves 5.2 points. The cheapest control in such a comparison is a second run of the same cell, the one most comparisons skip, and we recommend reporting it next to any harness gap.
